title: The Trade Season Is Open
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien uses the sports trade-window metaphor to reflect on teacher retention in term 4 of the Australian school year. He gives teachers a set of questions to ask when deciding whether to stay: is there room to grow, do teams trust each other, is leadership supportive, and does leadership actively work on workload. He notes that advancement can feel closed when it is not merit based and that educated teachers can end up as lone warlords in a failed state if leadership does not back evidence-informed practice. For school leaders he argues that some turnover is healthy but high turnover is a culture warning, and that schools control communication, development pathways, workload, and leadership support even if they cannot control commutes or friendships. He recommends transparent communication, individual performance development plans with regular check-ins, and using term 4 to pilot subtractions that reduce workload. The goal is a culture strong enough to outlast any individual departure.
points: Term 4 is the moment when teachers should ask honestly whether their school offers growth, trust, support, and respect for their time.
Advancement that feels based on relationships rather than merit is a red flag, and leaving to gain experience elsewhere can be the path back to a leadership seat.
Leaders can control communication, development avenues, workload, and support, so retention work should focus there rather than on commutes or social chemistry.
Individualised performance development plans with consistent check-ins give teachers meaningful goals that the annual school plan alone cannot provide.
Term 4 is a good time to pilot subtractions such as fewer checklists and communication platforms that free teachers to focus on teaching.
quotes: Do I feel like there is an avenue for growth and development for me here?
Advancement in schools is tricky as there are a finite amount of leadership positions and exponentially more teachers. It’s also important that advancement feels merit based.

Staff turnover within schools is not completely negative in nature. Some turnover is positive as it may bring in the missing puzzle piece that provides the expertise which the school may be missing with their current staffing profile
What schools can control is the flow of communication, clear avenues for development, teacher workload and the degree of leadership support.
Being upfront and transparent in as much communication and decision-making as possible goes a long way for staff to support even the less popular decisions being made.
If teachers within a school only have the goals within the schools annual implementation plans then it’s pretty close to having no goal at all.
Are staff being subjected to death by checklist in all of their administrative tasks? Are there too many communication platforms which are eating up their time?
